title: Longest Nice Subarray
statement: `nums` holds positive integers. A contiguous, non-empty block of `nums` is **nice** when, for any two of its elements taken from different positions, their bitwise AND is `0`; in other words, no bit is set in more than one of its elements. A block of a single element is always nice. Return the length of the longest nice block.
notes:
## Intuition

A block is nice exactly when its elements never share a set bit, so the OR of the block works as a record of which bits are taken. Checking every block pair by pair is O(n³). But niceness is preserved when a block shrinks, so a variable-size sliding window applies: grow the window on the right, and when the new number clashes with a bit already taken, drop numbers from the left until it fits. Because the elements of a nice window have disjoint bits, removing one is a plain XOR. Since a value below 10^9 has only 30 bits, a nice window can never be longer than 30.

## Approach

1. Keep `used`, the OR of the window `nums[left..right]`, plus `best`, the longest length seen.
2. For each `right`, while `used & nums[right]` is not 0, remove `nums[left]` with `used ^= nums[left]` and move `left` forward.
3. Now `nums[right]` shares no bit with the window: add it with `used |= nums[right]`.
4. Update `best` with the window length `right - left + 1`, and return it at the end.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [1, 3, 8, 48, 10]`. Taking 1 gives `used = 1`. 3 shares bit 0, so 1 leaves and `used = 3`. 8 and 48 fit: `used = 59`, window `[3, 8, 48]`, `best = 3`. 10 (binary 1010) clashes; removing 3 leaves `used = 56`, still clashing on bit 3, so 8 is removed too. With `used = 48`, 10 fits and the window `[48, 10]` has length 2. The answer is `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index enters and leaves the window at most once.
- Space: O(1): one mask and a few indices.

## Pitfalls

- Shrink the window before adding `nums[right]`: once a clashing value is ORed into `used`, the shared bit belongs to two numbers and XOR can no longer remove one of them cleanly.
- Write `(used & nums[right]) !== 0` with parentheses: `!==` binds tighter than `&` in JavaScript, Java and C.
- Equal values always clash (any positive value shares a bit with itself), so repeated numbers end the window.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `used` | OR of the values in the window: the bits already taken |
| `left`, `right` | first and last index of the current window |
| `best` | length of the longest nice window found |

narration.2: used holds every bit taken by the numbers in the current window.
narration.3: left is the first index of the window.
narration.5: Try to extend the window with each number in turn.
narration.6: While the new number shares a bit with the window, the window is not nice with it.
narration.7: The window's bits are disjoint, so XOR removes exactly the leftmost number's bits.
narration.8: Shrink the window from the left.
narration.10: No clash remains: add the new number's bits to the window.
narration.11: The window nums[left..right] is nice; keep the longest length.
narration.13: Return the longest nice window found.
